source.title: Avoiding Copyright Infringement via Large Language Model Unlearning
source.authors: Guang-Yao Dou; Zheyuan Liu; Qing Lyu; Kai-Ze Ding; Eric Wong

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results on previously unlearned book knowledge re-emerging during sequential unlearning on later books, refining the claim to a partial and setting-dependent recovery effect.
record.gate_note: The paper tests sequential unlearning, then measures whether knowledge of earlier books re-emerges as the model is unlearned on later, unrelated books. Its book-specific recovery evidence is described in text but the plotted values are not supplied numerically. Prompting and MemFree are tested as copyright-takedown methods, not as post-unlearning attacks. The paper does not test activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-only recovery after unlearning.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (sequential copyright unlearning of books), the study tracks per-book ROUGE-L of earlier-unlearned books. It finds the scores rise again as the model is fine-tuned with unlearning objectives on later, unrelated books (Appendix B.2, Figs 7–8). This is an indirect analogue of version B's unrelated-data fine-tuning recovery. Tables 2–17 also report how far each method lowers targeted ROUGE while keeping MMLU/MT-Bench, which bears on version A.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that SSU gives a better trade-off between unlearning efficacy and general ability than GA, Gradient Difference, TV, NPO, prompting and MemFree, and that prompting and MemFree barely mitigate copying. They note in Limitations and B.2 that previously unlearned book knowledge re-emerges at later steps under all tested algorithms. They link this to Łucki et al.'s unrelated-fine-tuning recovery and call for more robust methods.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates sequential book unlearning using task vectors, random-label loss, and weight saliency; its recovery evidence comes from later sequential training on other books, not the specified few-example, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery results vary by model and method; the paper specifically describes NPO increases for particular earlier books and only some reappearance under SSU.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama-3.1, Gradient Difference and SSU yield ROUGE on non-targeted books (Dnor) above the vanilla model (e.g. SSU t4 0.2417 vs 0.2349). The authors attribute this to knowledge redistribution or anticipatory recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning fine-tuning can raise reproduction of non-targeted memorized text above the pre-unlearning level.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL), 2024
record.problems: Book-specific recovery values are shown only in figures and are not given numerically in the text; no uncertainty estimates are reported. ROUGE is a lexical proxy, and the evidence concerns sequential unlearning on books rather than controlled recovery attacks or accuracy near chance.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; no additional recovery results were extracted from the aggregate Dprev tables because the evaluated set changes across sequential steps, making those aggregates insufficient to isolate recovery of the same earlier book.

untested.parts: Robustness of unlearning to the simple attacks named in A (dedicated relearning, ablation, quantization, prompting).

Recovery from a dedicated small relearning set (unrelated, related, or a subset of forgotten facts). Here the 'relearning' is only further unlearning on other books, and the magnitude of recovery is not quantified in the text.
All: no activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deletion.
All: quantization was explicitly not used (A.5) and is not tested as an attack.
All: prompting and MemFree are tested as takedown methods, not as recovery attacks.
All: SSU is not tested against recovery attacks, and it itself shows reappearance.

missing.what: Df ROUGE-1/ROUGE-L and MMLU/MT-Bench per method and time step. These show only small targeted reductions for capability-preserving methods and collapse for methods that reach ~0 ROUGE, which is the evidence for version A.
missing.locator: Appendix D, Tables 2–17; Section 6.1, 6.3; Appendix D.1–D.2

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: the paper makes no specific argument that a version is wrong; it reports re-emergence in a new sequential setting. The recovery evidence is weak for B because the unlearned starting point is barely below vanilla on ROUGE, so recovery of 'hidden' knowledge is small by construction. ROUGE is lexical with no chance level. None of the original sources is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The paper evaluates unlearning effectiveness and general abilities, but does not test the combined claim that targeted knowledge reaches near chance and simple attacks fail to recover it.

It tests re-emergence during sequential unlearning on later book data, not recovery from a specified small set of examples, loose related examples, or a subset of forgotten facts; the amount of recovery is not quantified in the described book-specific results.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis distinguishing blocked access from deleted knowledge is reported.
No post-unlearning quantization recovery test is reported.
No post-unlearning test of rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information is reported.
SSU is evaluated for sequential unlearning efficacy and retention, not for resistance to the recovery attacks in the claim.

statements.correction: This study reports no tamper-resistance or robustness add-on result and no with/without comparison. SSU 'exhibits some degree of reappearance' of earlier-unlearned books during sequential unlearning, with no model or magnitude stated. The authors say re-emergence occurs under all unlearning algorithms tested (Limitations, App. B.2). Remove this study from B.against[0].
statements.problem: The statement cites R4 as an example of a training-time tamper-resistance or robustness add-on that cuts recovery. SSU (random-label loss plus weight saliency) is a stability method for sequential unlearning, not a robustness add-on. The study compares no recovery with and without an add-on and gives no numbers. Its only finding here, that knowledge reappears, points toward version B, not against it.
